definition: Albert One is an artificial intelligence chatbot created by Robby Garner and designed to mimic the way humans make conversations using a multi-faceted approach in natural language programming.
details: Albert One is an artificial intelligence chatbot created by Robby Garner and designed to mimic the way humans make conversations using a multi-faceted approach in natural language programming.

explainer.lead: Albert One was Robby Garner’s chatbot, built from several cooperating programs and a growing collection of human statements and replies. It won the Loebner Prize Contest in both 1998 and 1999, showing how a hierarchy of relatively simple conversational parts could work together.

tiers.eli5: Albert One is like a small team trying to answer a visitor, with different helpers offering their own way of handling a conversation. It also has something like a giant notebook of things people say and possible replies. The team and notebook work together to choose what the computer says next.
tiers.practitioner: An engineer reconstructing this approach would coordinate several response programs hierarchically, then test database queries and assertions before producing an answer. Relevant settings include the internet data-gathering deployment begun in 1995 and the Loebner Prize contests. A key pitfall is treating Albert One as a single ELIZA-style program: its helper applications and statement–reply database were central to its behavior.
tiers.paperLevel: Schematically, response(x) = hierarchical_selection(ELIZA_like(x), helpers(x), queries_and_assertions(D, x)), where x is an input statement and D is the stimulus–response database. Its subsystems included a version of ELIZA, another ELIZA-like bot named Elivs, and additional helper applications. Evaluation was contest-based: parts were tested in the 1994–1997 Loebner Prize contests, and Albert One won in 1998 and 1999.

usedIn.name: Loebner Prize contests
usedIn.detail: The statement–reply portion was tested from 1994 through 1997, and Albert One won the contest in 1998 and 1999.

usedIn.name: Internet conversation collection
usedIn.detail: Parts of Albert were deployed online beginning in 1995 to learn what people would say to a chatterbot.

components.name: ELIZA subsystem
components.detail: A version of ELIZA, the therapist program, formed one part of the system.

components.name: Elivs
components.detail: This was another ELIZA-like conversational bot within Albert One.

components.name: Helper applications
components.detail: Several additional programs worked with the conversational bots in a hierarchical arrangement.

components.name: Stimulus–response library
components.detail: A large database associated human statements with possible replies.

components.name: Queries and assertions
components.detail: Database queries and assertions were tested to arrive at each response.

flow: A person’s statement enters Albert One’s hierarchical system.
The ELIZA version, Elivs, and helper applications work together on the conversation.
Database queries and assertions are tested against the stimulus–response material.
The system produces the resulting reply.
explainer.origin: Robby Garner created Albert One, with parts deployed on the internet beginning in 1995 to collect examples of what people said to a chatterbot. Its statement–reply database work was tested at the 1994–1997 Loebner Prize contests.
explainer.lineage: Albert was the first of Garner’s multifaceted bots and won the Loebner Prize in 1998 and 1999. Garner later developed networked examples of the same hierarchical “glue” approach at The Turing Hub.
explainer.whyItMatters: Albert One illustrates an early multi-component approach to conversation rather than reliance on a single response mechanism. Its successive Loebner Prize wins made that combination of conversational subsystems and collected human exchanges especially notable.

diagram.caption: Albert One combined several conversational subsystems with database tests to produce a response.
